lead: A steam power plant burns coal or gas to boil water, spins a turbine with the steam, and condenses the exhaust back to liquid so the loop can repeat. The four devices — pump, boiler, turbine, condenser — form the Rankine cycle. Almost all thermal electricity in India, whether from coal, nuclear or solar-thermal heat, comes from this cycle, so its efficiency decides how much fuel a unit burns for every kWh it sends out.
prereq: You need: the Carnot cycle, entropy, the steady-flow energy balance from the first-law chapters, and steam-table reading (thermodynamic property tables and diagrams).

sections.h3: Four devices in a closed loop

blocks.text: Water circulates. The pump takes saturated liquid from the condenser and raises its pressure to boiler pressure; the liquid temperature rises only a little because liquid water is nearly incompressible. The boiler adds heat at almost constant pressure: the water warms to saturation, boils, and is usually superheated. The turbine expands the high-pressure steam and delivers shaft work, so pressure and temperature fall. The condenser rejects heat at constant pressure and temperature, turning the exhaust back into saturated liquid.

For each device the steady-flow energy balance, with kinetic and potential energy neglected, gives q − w = Δh. With the state numbers of the figure: turbine work w<sub>t</sub> = h₃ − h₄, pump work w<sub>p</sub> = h₂ − h₁, boiler heat q<sub>in</sub> = h₃ − h₂ and condenser heat q<sub>out</sub> = h₄ − h₁, all in kJ per kg of water. Here w<sub>t</sub> and w<sub>p</sub> are positive magnitudes: w<sub>t</sub> is delivered, w<sub>p</sub> is absorbed (in q − w = Δh the pump has w = −w<sub>p</sub>).

A Carnot cycle between the same temperatures would be more efficient, but it cannot be built for steam: it would have to compress a wet mixture. The Rankine cycle condenses fully and pumps only liquid, which needs a small pump; the price is a lower mean temperature of heat addition.

On the T–s diagram of the figure the saturated liquid and vapour lines form the dome. Pump work 1→2 is a short, nearly vertical line on the liquid side. Boiler heating 2→3 runs along the 4 MPa line to superheated steam. Isentropic expansion 3→4 is a vertical drop into the wet region. Condensation 4→1 is a horizontal line at 45.8 °C.

The thermal efficiency compares net work out with heat paid for in the boiler. The pump work is small compared with turbine work, but it is real work bought from the same shaft, so it must be subtracted.
η = (w<sub>t</sub> − w<sub>p</sub>) / q<sub>in</sub> = [(h₃ − h₄) − (h₂ − h₁)] / (h₃ − h₂)
blocks.where: η is the cycle thermal efficiency (dimensionless); h₃ is turbine-inlet enthalpy, h₄ turbine-exit enthalpy, h₁ condenser-exit (pump-inlet) enthalpy, h₂ pump-exit (boiler-inlet) enthalpy, all in kJ/kg.

items: Fix the boiler pressure p<sub>b</sub> and the condenser pressure p<sub>c</sub>.
At the turbine inlet (state 3) take the known pressure and temperature, read h₃ and s₃ from the superheated steam table.
For an ideal turbine, s₄ = s₃ at pressure p<sub>c</sub>; find quality x₄ = (s₃ − s<sub>f</sub>)/s<sub>fg</sub>, then h₄ = h<sub>f</sub> + x₄ h<sub>fg</sub>.
Pump work for liquid: w<sub>p</sub> ≈ v<sub>f</sub> (p<sub>b</sub> − p<sub>c</sub>), with v<sub>f</sub> in m³/kg and pressures in kPa, giving kJ/kg. Then h₂ = h₁ + w<sub>p</sub>.
Boiler heat q<sub>in</sub> = h₃ − h₂, net work w<sub>net</sub> = (h₃ − h₄) − w<sub>p</sub>, and η = w<sub>net</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>.

blocks.text: Real machines fall short. Turbine isentropic efficiency η<sub>t</sub> = (h₃ − h₄)/(h₃ − h₄s) is about 0.85 to 0.92, so the actual exit has higher entropy, higher enthalpy and more moisture than the ideal one. Pump isentropic efficiency is 0.70 to 0.85, but because w<sub>p</sub> is only 1 to 3 percent of turbine work, its uncertainty barely moves the cycle efficiency.

Typical large utility values: boiler at 100 bar and 540 °C, condenser at 0.1 bar, where the saturation temperature is 45.8 °C. The ideal cycle gives about 41 percent; with an 85 percent turbine it drops to about 35 percent, and reheat and feed heating win part of the loss back.

items: Reheat: expand to an intermediate pressure, send the steam back to the boiler to reheat at constant pressure, then expand again. The mean temperature of heat addition rises a little, and the exhaust stays drier (quality above about 0.88), which protects the last blades.

Regenerative feed heating: bleed a fraction of steam from the turbine at several points and use it to warm the feedwater in open (mixing) or closed heaters. The boiler then receives hotter water, so q<sub>in</sub> falls for the same turbine output. Bleeding removes steam that would have made work, so the gain is real but bounded; large units use several heaters in series.

Condenser pressure: a lower p<sub>c</sub> lowers the temperature of heat rejection and raises efficiency. The limit is the cooling water available (river or cooling-tower water near 30 °C), air leaking into the vacuum, and the length of the last blades.

blocks.text: Raising boiler pressure also raises efficiency, but it pushes the turbine exhaust deeper into the wet region, so higher pressure goes together with superheat and reheat. Supercritical units run above the critical pressure of water, 220.6 bar, where there is no boiling stage at all.

figure.caption: The worked example on temperature–entropy axes, with the saturation dome of water. The pump (1→2) hardly shows, the boiler line 2→3 heats, boils at 250.4 °C and superheats to 400 °C, the ideal turbine drops straight to 4 at x = 0.816, and the real 85 % turbine ends to the right at 4a: more entropy, a drier exhaust (x = 0.883) and less work.

examples.question: An ideal Rankine cycle has steam at 4 MPa and 400 °C entering the turbine and a condenser at 10 kPa. Steam-table values: at 4 MPa, 400 °C, h₃ = 3214.4 kJ/kg and s₃ = 6.7712 kJ/(kg·K); at 10 kPa, h<sub>f</sub> = 191.8 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 0.6492 kJ/(kg·K), s<sub>fg</sub> = 7.4997 kJ/(kg·K), v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001010 m³/kg. Find the pump work, turbine work, heat added, efficiency and heat rejected. Then find the efficiency if the turbine is 85 % efficient.
steps: State 1 (saturated liquid at 10 kPa): h₁ = 191.8 kJ/kg. Pump: w<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>f</sub>(p<sub>b</sub> − p<sub>c</sub>) = 0.001010 × (4000 − 10) = 4.03 kJ/kg, so h₂ = 191.8 + 4.0 = 195.8 kJ/kg.
q<sub>out</sub> = h₄ − h₁ = 2144.5 − 191.8 = 1952.7 kJ/kg. Check: q<sub>in</sub> − q<sub>out</sub> = 1065.9 kJ/kg = w<sub>net</sub>.
examples.answer: w<sub>p</sub> = 4.0 kJ/kg, w<sub>t</sub> = 1069.9 kJ/kg, q<sub>in</sub> = 3018.6 kJ/kg, η = 35.3 % and q<sub>out</sub> = 1952.7 kJ/kg; with an 85 % turbine η falls to 30.0 %.

traps: Using turbine work alone as net work. Subtract the pump work: w<sub>net</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − w<sub>p</sub>.
Taking q<sub>in</sub> from the condenser exit enthalpy h₁. The boiler receives feedwater after the pump, so use h₂ = h₁ + w<sub>p</sub>.
Mixing bar, kPa and MPa in w<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>f</sub> Δp. Convert pressure difference to kPa so that v<sub>f</sub> in m³/kg gives kJ/kg directly.
Confusing turbine isentropic efficiency (actual against ideal expansion) with cycle efficiency (net work against boiler heat).

Saying the condenser temperature stays constant throughout. It stays at T<sub>sat</sub> only while the steam is wet; if the condensate is subcooled, the last part of the condenser cools liquid below saturation.

quiz.q: Name the four devices of a Rankine cycle and state what each does to the water.
quiz.a: Pump raises pressure of liquid water; boiler adds heat at nearly constant pressure and makes steam; turbine expands steam and produces work; condenser rejects heat and turns exhaust back into saturated liquid.

quiz.q: Why is a Rankine cycle used instead of a Carnot cycle in steam plants, even though Carnot is more efficient?
quiz.a: A Carnot cycle would need compression of a wet two-phase mixture with an enormous compressor. Rankine condenses fully in the condenser and pumps only liquid, which needs a small, cheap pump. The loss in efficiency is accepted for a buildable plant.

quiz.q: Why does lowering the condenser pressure raise the cycle efficiency?
quiz.a: It lowers the saturation temperature at which heat is rejected (45.8 °C at 10 kPa, 32.9 °C at 5 kPa). The turbine expands to a lower pressure, so w<sub>t</sub> rises, while q<sub>in</sub> rises only a little because h₁ and h₂ fall slightly. Net work rises more than q<sub>in</sub>, so η rises; in Carnot terms the mean temperature of heat rejection has fallen.

quiz.q: Steam enters a turbine at h = 3400 kJ/kg and leaves at h = 2200 kJ/kg. The condensate enthalpy is 200 kJ/kg and the pump work is 10 kJ/kg. Find the cycle efficiency.
Two plants work between the same boiler and condenser pressures; one uses reheat and the other does not. Explain why the reheat plant is more efficient and why its turbine blades last longer.
quiz.a: Reheat adds part of the heat at a higher temperature, raising the mean temperature of heat addition, so the same heat produces more work. It also reduces the moisture at the turbine exhaust, and dry-ish steam erodes the last-stage blades far less than wet steam.

quiz.q: A simple cycle at 100 bar and 500 °C exhausts to 0.1 bar. Explain why the exhaust is wet, and state two changes that would reduce the moisture.
quiz.a: Isentropic expansion from 100 bar and 500 °C (s = 6.60 kJ/(kg·K)) to 0.1 bar, where s<sub>g</sub> = 8.15 kJ/(kg·K), ends inside the dome: x ≈ 0.79 for an ideal turbine. To dry it, superheat the inlet steam further, or reheat at an intermediate pressure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Supercritical units run above 220.6 bar with no boiling stage, ultra-supercritical units push steam above 600 °C, and combined cycles add a gas turbine on top of the steam cycle. Search for "supercritical Rankine cycle" and "combined cycle power plant".
